strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: missing protected attributes can distort fairness estimates and undermine fair GNN training. Adversarial imputation is an interesting approach to this problem.

The reported BAIL results are promising. With GCN, BFtS improves F1 from FairGNN’s 0.86 to 0.907 and reduces equality-of-opportunity disparity from 4.1% to 1.7%. GERMAN also shows substantial fairness improvements, with some predictive-performance loss.
Experiments cover three real datasets, synthetic graphs, GCN and GAT architectures, relevant baselines, ten runs, fairness–accuracy comparisons, and partial ablations. A code repository is linked.
weaknesses: The central worst-case interpretation is not established. Equation (8) optimizes cross-entropy and covariance over learned sensitive labels without defining admissible imputations or showing a connection to worst-case demographic parity or equality of opportunity. Changing group proportions can make sensitive labels easier to predict without increasing representation bias. The paper needs evidence against degenerate imputations and direct comparisons of fairness measured using imputed versus true attributes.

The contribution is not adequately isolated from FairGNN. FairGNN already contains a classifier, sensitive-attribute estimator, and adversary; BFtS principally changes the estimator’s objective and introduces LDAM. Table 3 only ablates the fairness losses. LDAM-matched FairGNN, BFtS with cross-entropy classification, and a nonadversarial imputer control are needed to attribute the gains to the proposed mechanism.

The training specification contains material inconsistencies. Figure 2’s caption says the imputer maximizes L_A, whereas Equation (8) minimizes it. Algorithm 1 references Equations (2) and (4) for classifier and imputer updates, omitting the adversarial terms in Equations (6) and (8). Equation (5) also describes conversion to binary predictions without explaining how differentiability is retained.

The missingness experiments do not address the main motivating scenario of biased data collection. The selection mechanism for observed protected attributes is unspecified, and varying their observed fraction from 20% to 50% does not establish robustness to group-dependent or feature-dependent missingness. These mechanisms require explicit evaluation.

Quantitative reporting needs reconciliation. Table 3 labels the synthetic DP and EQOP values 0.72 and 0.08 as percentages, while Figure 3 shows approximately 70% and 8%, suggesting inconsistent units. The exceptionally small reported uncertainty values are also not identified as standard deviations, standard errors, or another statistic.

Important experimental details are missing, including complete training/validation/test partitions, optimizer settings, hyperparameter ranges and selected values, training budgets, and the precise model-selection rule combining AVPR and F1. Figure 4 also contains operating points where FairGNN or RNF performs better, so the broader trade-off advantage needs more controlled comparisons. Together with the unresolved attribution and methodological issues, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier conference.
